subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE IN "BOATING" MAGAZINE BY COMMANDER A. D. MACLEAN (RETIRED)

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): Mr. Speaker, a few days ago the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group (Mr. Coldwell) and the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Graydon) placed questions
488	COMMONS
Canadian Navy-"Boating" Magazine
on Hansard, and asked for a statement in regard to an article entitled "Fairmiles and Foul" which appears in the January-February issue of a magazine called Boating. I regret that some time elapsed before I was able to gather together all the information necessary to make a full statement, and I regret still further that the statement itself must occupy some little time. But the article in question, together with editorials and other articles in the January-February issue of Boating, occupied practically the whole magazine, and it has been necessary to traverse a good deal of ground in order to be able to make an appropriate reply.	,
The article purports to criticize the building and manning of Fairmile boats in Canada and their operation by the Royal Canadian Navy. The article was written by Andrew D. MacLean, Commander R.C.N.Y.R., retired. It is quite a long article. In places it expresses the writer's opinion. In others it purports to state facts. I shall not attempt to deal with every statement of opinion or with every insinuation contained in the article. I shall deal chiefly with what the writer alleges to be facts, and I shall make such comments on these allegations as I can make from my own knowledge or from information supplied to me by officials of my department or by other reliable sources.
Training of crews. One of the first statements which Commander MacLean makes is with regard to the training of crews for these Fairmiles. On the very first page of his article, page 7 of the magazine, he says:
The senior officers of the Canadian. Navy prefer to run things in their own particularly obscure manner. .. .and make no difference between the training of Fairmile crews and the maintenance of the 600 h.p. Hall-Scott engines than they do for men and the steam machinery of corvettes, minesweepers and destroyers.
Again, on page 9, he says:
No special training was given our officers or men on being accepted volunteers for the Fairmiles service.
These are some of Commander MacLean's statements, and I should like to point out what the facts are. The facts are that before any Fairmiles were completed in Canada, engine-room crews were given special training in the running and maintenance of Hall-Scott engines, which are the engines used in these boats. Beginning early in 1941 and going on until February, 1942, two engineer lieutenants, one warrant engineer and fifty-four specially selected chief motor mechanics were sent to the Hall-Scott works in Berkeley, California, to undergo a complete course in the management

of the Hall-Scott type of engine. The men who were given this special training had, prior to their entry in the Canadian Navy, considerable experience with internal combustion engines, such as the Hall-Scott engines are. Upon completing this course one of these men was detailed to stand by each Canadian Fairmile as the machinery was being installed. One of these men was also a part of the crew of each vessel commissioned. As the shore repair staffs for Fairmiles at Halifax and Esquimalt became more familiar with the maintenance and operation of the Fairmile machinery, it was found that training which formerly had to be undertaken in California could now be efficiently conducted in this country, and accordingly the practice of sending men to California was discontinued.
In addition to this training in the maintenance and operation of Fairmile machinery, the naval mechanical training establishments at Halifax, Esquimalt and Pietou ran special courses in internal combustion machinery. This was general training for the class of engine to which the Hall-Scott belongs.
On page 9 of the article Commander MacLean says:
By August, 1942, out of more than thirty boats in commission only ten were fit for operational duties as a direct result of Ottawa's failure to provide specialized training and adequate, specialized base facilities.
The fact is that in August, 1942, there was a completely adequate number of trained men available to operate each Fairmile then in commission. In addition there was an adequate number of replacements available to take care of any emergency which might have arisen. A special branch of the Canadian Navy had been established for internal combustion engine ships. This branch corresponds to the regular stoker branch in the navy.
Providing crews before boats are ready. The second allegation with which I should like to deal is that in the autumn of 1941, twelve officers and seventy-two men waited at Toronto for some six weeks before they could actually man the ships and bring them down through the lake and river to the east coast.
It must be pointed out here that it is very common practice to send some officers and key ratings to every new ship some time before the ship is accepted. It is obvious, I think, to anyone who reflects upon the matter that men cannot arrive on a new ship, accept her, commission her and begin to operate her

Canadian Navy-"Boating" Magazine
all in one day. Some considerable period of instruction and of getting acquainted with the machinery is necessary.
The Fairmiles to which Commander MacLean refers in this instance were launched in July and August, 1941. We fully expected that they would be ready for acceptance much earlier than they actually were ready. Delays were caused by the difficulty in securing equipment, some of which had to be got in the United States, and it was not until the first days in November that the ships could actually be taken over by the Canadian Navy and sailed for the east coast.
Commander MacLean goes on to say that in the spring of 1942, "twelve boats had complete crews provided three months before they were needed, or 192 officers and men with nothing to do for ninety days." My information is that this statement is directly contrary to the fact, and some reflection would seem to show that my information is correct. The month of May is the first month in which wooden ships, not large ships, either, as these Fairmiles are, could safely leave great lakes ports for the east coast. If Commander MacLean's statement is correct, it would mean that complete crews for these twelve boats had been sent to the lakes in the month of February, when the rivers and lakes are completely frozen over.
Paying off Fairmile crews. Commander MacLean goes on to say that the crews of five boats were paid off in Halifax in December, 1941, "because of an artificial shortage of officers created by the opening of special schools before we had enough people to man the ships so urgently needed at sea." My reply to that statement is this, that the Canadian navy had to make the best disposition possible out of the men it had in the service.
Its principal task then was, and still is, that of escort work across the Atlantic. That is work which Fairmiles cannot undertake, at least for a transatlantic voyage. Corvettes and other ships of that type were urgently required for this duty, and so, too, were officers and men to man them. In December, 1941, training facilities were not available to the same extent as they are to-day, and in view of the shortages of personnel, the manning commander at Halifax had to use the available men on the ships where they were most urgently needed. Hence it was not the opening of special schools which deprived Fair-miles of crews in the winter of 1941. It was the urgent need of personnel for the larger ships which could be used as transatlantic escorts.
Dinghies for Fairmiles. Commander MacLean then refers to the dinghy supplied for these Fairmiles, and says that it was a joke. "Heavy beyond belief, it would not handle under oars or sail and was unsafe with more than two people on board."
The dinghies supplied for the Fairmiles were built, just as the Fairmiles were built, in accordance with designs worked out by the British Admirality. It is not true to say that they would not handle under oars or sail. In this instance Commander MacLeaD is giving an opinion, but I prefer to take against his opinion the view of the director of naval operations, Captain H. N. Lay, an officer of vastly greater naval experience than Commander MacLean, and an officer who has won two decorations in this war for his gallantry in actual naval operations. Captain Lay paid a visit to the shipyards building Fairmiles in the month of October, 1941, and he reports as follows:
I took particular notice of the ten feet dinghies which are supplied to the Fairmiles built. This boat is an extremely well built one, very strongly constructed, and should stand up very well to the handling it will receive during service. It is slightly on the heavy side, but as a davit is fitted for lowering, it is considered that this is an advantage rather than a disadvantage.
Guns for Fairmiles. The next allegation of Commander MacLean deals with guns. He says this on page 9 of his article:
The guns supplied were from eighteen to thirty years old and the ammunition of United States origin and very doubtful history. . .
As in the case of the dinghies, the guns supplied to Fairmiles were the same as those specified by the Admiralty for the same class of boats built for the Royal Navy. The guns for the Fairmile boats were obtained originally, in part from the Admiralty and in part from the United States Navy. The type of gun fitted to our Fairmiles was the one deliberately planned to be fitted, as laid down in the plans and specifications received from the British Admiralty. It is not a question here, Mr. Speaker, of having the perfect gun. It is a question of taking the best that you can get at the time.
But since the Fairmiles were originally armed, now nearly two years ago, I am happy to say that a better type of gun has become available, and is being fitted in the Fairmiles. I say further that the problem of securing better armament for these Fairmile boats and for all other types of ships used in the Canadian navy is one which is constantly under review by competent gunnery experts and armament specialists. These men are in touch

490	COMMONS
Canadian Navy-Boating" Magazine
with the Royal Navy on the subject all the time, and whenever better armament is available for any Canadian ship, it is procured.
To illustrate the attitude which Commander MacLean has adopted throughout the article, I should like to refer to a photograph on page eleven, which he captions:
Lesson in Fire Power for the R.C.N.
Picture shows Fairmile of the Royal Navy on patrol in the North sea.
I am advised and I believe that the vessel shown in the photograph is not the same type of vessel we use at all; it is a Fairmile of a totally different class, one used against German E-boats, whereas our Fairmile is used against submarines. I think it is strange that Commander MacLean, who sets himself up as a great expert on Fairmiles, should make so grievous a mistake as that.
Electrical equipment. Then he deals with the question of electrical equipment and complains that in Canada we have maintained the English standard voltage of 24 instead of the north American standard of 32 or 110 on our Fairmiles. It may be said in reply to this charge that the electrical supply of 24 volts is not only in accordance with Admiralty design, but was also determined by the voltage of the generators supplied with the main engines. There was no option in the matter. We had to take the generators as they were or go without them.
It is true that two increases in electrical power supply have had to be made on these boats, but these changes were made necessary by the introduction and development of new equipment since the original Fairmiles were designed. It must be remembered that the present-day supply of electrical equipment is very limited indeed, and the retention of the 24 volt and the introduction of the additional 110 volt systems were the most feasible and economical and the only practical arrangements which could be made in the circumstances.
The Lynx. Then Commander MacLean refers to the breaking-up of the Lynx. The Lynx was one of the yachts which the navy procured in the early days of the war and converted for naval purposes. He says, on page 30, that he was appointed to command the Lynx, which was to be the mother ship of certain Fairmiles, that shortly after his appointment he went on leave, and that on his return the Lynx was being broken up for scrap metal. He goes on to say, "A signal had been misread."
Nothing could illustrate the unreliability of this gentleman any more clearly than this statement about the Lynx. While the Lynx,

which was a very old yacht, had been condemned as unseaworthy and unsafe and unfit for service, and while her machinery had been taken out, she was not being broken up at the time that Commander MacLean returned from leave, nor has she since been broken up for scrap metal. She is still lying at a dock in a certain eastern Canadian port.
Delays in building. Commander MacLean complains next of the great delays that occurred in the building of these Fairmiles, due, as he claims, to lack of intelligent priorities on engines, tanks and fittings. He says that it takes two to three times as long to build these boats in Canada as it does in Britain.
I should be the last to deny that there have been delays in the shipbuilding programme for Fairmiles. Here, it must be remembered, there was a new industry for Canada. New sources of supply had to be developed; new materials and new machinery had to be secured. Shipyards had to be built in some cases and their staffs had to be organized in almost all cases. There is bound to be delay in any countrjr in such circumstances, but I must point out that in Great Britain several desighs of Fairmiles are produced, whereas Canada produces only one type, and that is the Fairmile used in anti-submarine work.
In Britain, again, boats are built on the mass production principle, but even with this mass production method it takes from five to six months to build a Fairmile in Great Britain. In this country, as I said before, we built and are building Fairmiles to the British design. The first contract wTas let on December 17,	1940. The contractors
were required to build the hulls only. The department supplied special equipment and machinery. In procuring this equipment and machinery very many difficulties and delays were encountered.
In a war where there are great demands upon every form of mechanical production, difficulties and delays are inevitable at first. I believe, however, that any shipbuilder building Fairmile boats will say that so far as the naval service is concerned it has done its utmost to help out the situation. For example, in the first month of the building programme, representatives of the naval service met with the contractors, with the builders of these boats, to clear up certain problems that were presented by the plans and specifications, and this contact with the builders has been maintained ever since. There are on file at naval service headquarters many letters expressing the builders'

Canadian Navy-"Boating" Magazine
appreciation of the help received from the naval service, and I have seen no letter or communication of any kind to the contrary.
As to the comparisons between the rate of building in this country and in England, as I have said, England employs the mass production method and even by that method it takes from five to six months to build a boat there. In Ontario, where most of these boats were built in the lake yards, from the time the first keels were laid, early in 1941, until the boats were commissioned, the average building time was eight and a half months. In the case of one firm, the time taken was six months and six days, and last year, 1942, one firm delivered one of these vessels in three months and twelve days from the laying of the keel. This is a splendid tribute to the zeal and skill of our shipbuilders.
Idle shipyards. The editorial which appears in the magazine Boating, on page 6, states that "of the five Fairmile building yards in Ontario, two are very busy and three have no Fairmiles to build." The facts are that there are seven Fairmile yards in Ontario, and in all seven yards Fairmiles are in various stages of construction at this very moment to the total number of ten.
Delivery of engines. In the article, Commander MacLean alleges that engines were delivered to some yards six months ahead of time, and in other cases the builders could not get engines when they required them. I will say, in answer to that, that there is no case known to me or to the department where engines were delivered to yards six months before they were required. As the engines were received by the navy at Toronto, they were shipped to the builders whose vessels were in the most advanced stage. There were some cases where builders who originally had been rather backward eventually made more rapid progress, and some of these builders might have had to wait a short time for engines, but never for six months.
Attack on Royal Canadian Navy. So much for the specific charges which Commander MacLean makes. But there is another matter to which I must refer, and it is this. Throughout the whole article, as well as in an editorial comment, and in anpther article appearing on pages 40 and 41, numerous slighting references are made to the Royal Canadian Navy, that is to say to the permanent force. It is suggested, for example, that the naval board should have more naval reserve and naval volunteer reserve representation.
In this connection, I should like to observe that the board of admiralty in Britain has no reserve officers on it. The Canadian naval board is modelled on the British board of 72537-324
admiralty, with this difference, however, that the board of admiralty is an executive body whereas the Canadian naval board is a body advisory to the minister of naval services. The minister, under the act, has full executive authority corresponding to the authority exercised in England, by the board of admiralty itself. But there is one further difference which Commander MacLean, or the editorial writer, has forgotten, and that is that the secretary of the naval board here is an officer of the naval volunteer reserve, whereas in Britain the secretary is a permanent civil servant.
The Canadian naval board consists of the chief of naval staff, the vice-chief of naval staff, the chief of naval engineering and construction, the chief of naval personnel, the chief of naval equipment and supply, the deputy minister of naval services, with a naval volunteer reserve officer as secretary.
It is alleged in this magazine that the board has awarded promotions and decorations to itself and to the personnel of the Royal Canadian Navy in a very improper and unfair manner. I must point out in answer to that charge that in the last promotions list which appeared at New Year's 3-1 per cent of the permanent R.C.N. officers received promotions, 10-5 per cent of the R.C.N.R. received promotions, and 4 per cent of the R.C.N.V.R. officers received promotions. In other words, the permanent R.C.N. officers received proportionately fewer promotions than either of the other two branches of the service. But beyond that, the naval board does not make promotions. Recommendations for promotions are made, in the first instance, by officers commanding ships and establishments. They are in the best possible position to know the merits of those serving under them. Their recommendations are then reviewed by the promotions board, which is a totally different board from the naval board, and finally the recommendations of the promotions board are reviewed by the minister, who has to make the final decision as to promotions.
So far as decorations are concerned, 84 have gone to members of the R.C.N., 54 to members of the R.C.N.R., and 123 to members of the R.C.N.V.R. It must be pointed out with regard to both promotions and decorations, that at the beginning of the war we had a very small navy. The ships were commanded and manned almost entirely by officers and men of the permanent force.. They were the first officers and men to see action, and I think I can safely say that they were all keen to get into action. It took some time to develop officers and men in the

Canadian Navy-"Boating" Magazine
two reserve branches. The profession of a naval officer, as I have often said to this house, is not one in which skill can be acquired in a day, or a week, or a month; it is a matter of years of training and experience.
In the first days of the war, therefore, inevitably the brunt of the work fell upon members of the permanent force. I am glad to say that now members of the two reserves, having gained valuable experience, are taking their places nobly, gallantly, in the battle line, and as time goes on and the navy increases in size, more and more of the work will fall on their shoulders. But I know of no officer in the permanent service who would not gladly go to sea at this instant if the opportunity presented itself.
It is alleged that we have too many high-ranking officers in the Canadian navy, too many admirals, too many brass hats. The Australian navy, which is only about one-half the size of the Canadian navy, I notice has five officers above the rank of captain, while we have seven. In comparison with the British navy it can be said that we are not too heavily staffed in the higher ranks. Indeed I think we are below the United Kingdom standard, for in the United Kingdom there are some . one hundred and eighteen admirals while we have five, which is a definitely smaller proportion.
I shall say nothing on the general question of the propriety of such articles as those that appear in the January-February issue of Boating, beyond this, that several of the statements may well be deemed to constitute an offence against the defence of Canada regulations. Such matters as details of the construction of ships, and the armament of ships, are not matters that, in time of war at least, are usually made the subject of newspaper or magazine articles. More especially is this true when a person acquires knowledge of these matters in the course of his service as an officer.
Above and beyond these particular matters I think I must say something, although I say it with some reluctance, about the writer of the article himself. I believe that is necessary, because many people who have read his article, even though they may hear or read what I have to say to-day, may still feel that there must be something wrong somewhere when a former officer takes what ought to be the very serious step of attacking his own service.
Let me say on this point that the total number of persons employed in Fairmiles at this time is under one thousand, and this out of a total strength of something more

than fifty thousand. So that with every consideration in the world for what the Fairmile fleet has done, and with every appreciation of the gallantry and fidelity of its members, the Fairmile fleet after all constitutes in men something less than one-fifitieth of the total strength of the Canadian navy.
Now a word about the author, because his experience and ability are proper matters for consideration in a case of this kind. He has criticized the ability and the judgment of others; he cannot blame us if we look now at his own talents and his own training.
Commander MacLean is now in his forty-seventh year. He has reached an age when service in small ships becomes very trying, as we have found by unfortunate experience with many officers who have passed beyond the vigour and resilience of youth. He served in the last war with the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve for a little over two years, first as a probationary sub-lieutenant and latterly as a lieutenant. His service was mostly in small craft in the Mediterranean sea and his record was good. He commanded the Toronto division of the R.C.N.V.R. from 1927 to 1931, when he retired. In 1935 he was made a lieutenant-commander on the retired list. Just before the outbreak of this war he offered his services to the Canadian navy. Subsequently, no place having been found for him in the Canadian navy at the time, he became attached to the Canadian air force. However, during the first nine months of the war he had considerable correspondence with the naval department, with the result that on July 13, 1940, he was offered an appointment as lieutenant-commander. But he thought this rank was not high enough to induce him to leave the air force, where he was a flight lieutenant. He felt that he should be a commander. He was told that there was no such appointment available, and he finally agreed to accept an appointment as lieutenant-commander. In this capacity he took charge of a group of yachtsmen going to England, and he arrived there on September 23, 1940.
After spending some time at bases there, he was given command of a coastal trawler, and in December, 1940, he was appointed to the staff of rear admiral coastal command. From January to June, 1941, he was on the staff of captain of motor launches at a United Kingdom port. The whole time which he spent at sea in United Kingdom waters in this war could not have exceeded two or three months; I think that is a generous estimate. He returned to Canada in August, 1941.

Canadian Navy-"Boating" Magazine
At this point reference must again be made to certain parts of his article. For instance, on page 8 he states that he was sent back to Canada to help with the Fairmile subchasers that were building. There is no record whatever to show that he was sent back to Canada or asked for by Canada for this purpose. Later on in the article he refers to his experience as acceptance officer of the British Admiralty on Fairmile motor launches. I communicated with the British Admiralty on this point, and I am informed by them that though he was on the staff of the captain of motor launches and though he would have had certain duties in connection with Fairmiles under construction, he was never admiralty acceptance officer for this type of craft.
When he returned to Canada we did not have any reports on him from Great Britain, and, as one Canadian officer put it in making a report of Commander MacLean's ability later on, "we had to take him largely at his own valuation." At any rate we took him and placed him in charge of Fairmiles as senior officer Fairmiles. He was given a set of definite instructions and told to go ahead. He held this post as senior officer Fairmiles for nine months. If the Fairmile situation is as bad as he says it is, should not he as senior officer in those formative months bear at least some of the blame?
I pass on now to what is perhaps the most significant comment I have to make. I have looked over all the files relating to Commander MacLean and to his service, both in Canada and in England. He has sneered at and belittled the Canadian navy so violently and so openly; he has lauded the British navy so highly-and quite properly lauded it-that I expected to find in his records something to indicate that he stood very high indeed in the opinion of officials of the great British navy. But what did I actually find? I found that his standing in British naval circles was exactly the opposite of high. The reports by his senior Canadian officers are not very flattering, but one of them at least is absolutely fulsome when compared with the reports by officers of the royal navy. Some time in 1941, in answer to a request that he be given some sea service, he was told in England that an endeavour would be made to send him to sea, but that he would not be considered for a command. These facts from the record, from the opinions of British and Canadian officers alike, together with the fact that his experience at sea in this war is quite limited, I think will have to be borne in mind in valuing his article.
I have only one word more to say. Boating has an editorial in the same issue suggesting that the House of Commons should order an inquiry into the administration of the navy. Remember, about a year ago the same magazine was threatened by a naval officer with a libel suit, and had to offer an apology for making incorrect statements. But I may inform Boating that if this House of Commons, wishes to order an inqury into the administration of the navy, either in respect of Fair-miles or in any other particular, I shall be quite content, and I have no fear whatever of the result.
I have always conceived the main function! of the Canadian navy up to the present to>
be that of convoy work in the north Atlantic-. It has other tasks on our coasts and on other seas, and as this house knows, more recently its work has been extended to the Mediterranean sea, where some Canadian ships of war-we were told yesterday that we had none-have already gained great distinction for themselves, and where unfortunately one has already met its end with a loss of thirty-five lives. The value of our naval contribution up to the present stands or falls on that work. A few weeks ago I stated publicly that more than forty per cent of the burden of escorting convoys from these shores to the United Kingdom falls on the ships, officers and men of the Royal Canadian Navy. That is the most precious, the most vital line in the world to-day, the line that runs from America to the United Kingdom, and more than forty per cent of the work of guarding that line falls on Canadian naval officers and men.
No matter what individuals may be attacked, ministers, chiefs of staff or other naval officers; no matter what innuendos may be cast or opinions offered, one fact will remain outstanding, namely, that to organize and carry out such a programme from small beginnings and under the stress of war conditions is not a minor contribution to the war effort; it is not the sort of contribution that is made by inefficient, incompetent or careless men.

Defence during the debate on the war appropriation bill, that after all these men and these departments are not infallible. We must not get into the habit of lightly tossing aside every suggestion with respect to the betterment of these services which already are doing good jobs, even though we may sometimes be termed arm-chair critics in war time. It is possible that these departments may render even better service. It is not my desire therefore to speak from any narrow point of view or to belittle any of our services.
I do not apologize to the minister for having suggested that he should make a full statement with regard to this article. I think that is the stand the country would expect to be taken by the leader of an opposition.
I was interested, of course, in the defence Lo the charges put forward by the minister. Upon one point he raised I should like to [DOT]comment further; that is, his suggestion that rthis was a serious step for Commander MacLean to take. I know nothing of what may have been the underlying motive in this case, because I merely read the article and must go by that entirely, but I agree with the minister that it was a step which this man must have known when he took it. But when the minister suggests that this article may contravene some provision of the defence of Canada regulations, then I say that he has said either too much or too little. During the last seven or eight months we have had an experience in Canada with respect to charges laid under the defence of Canada regulations. If this article, or these charges, by Commander MacLean actually contravene the defence of Canada regulations in any way it is the duty of the minister and the duty of the government to prosecute both the magazine and the author of this article to the full extent of the law. We as members of this house must realize, I think, that we cannot allow men, no matter how high they may stand in naval circles or in public life,, to contravene or offend against the defence of Canada regulations. The minister must now make up his mind with respect to the position he is to take. I should like to ask him if, in view of the .eerious charges which have been preferred,
IMr. Graydon.]
this matter has been referred to the Department of Justice for an opinion, as would ordinarily have been done.
What I say is not said in defence of the author of this article. I have no desire to defend anyone at the moment with respect to these charges. I am only anxious to have one thing happen. If there is something that can be done to make our naval board and our whole naval contribution in this war more effective and more nearly perfect, that should be the sole aim and object of every one of us. We must not indulge in carping or quibbling criticism of our navy, and I do not want that to be done. If there is something to this, then I think we must utilize it for the benefit of Canada and for the benefit of the navy on this particular occasion.
I am informed that on October 28, 1942, there was issued from naval services headquarters a release with respect to the retirement of this man. I know nothing about his record other than what the minister has told us; consequently I have no desire to dilate upon that. However, the press release from naval headquarters did say

I point this out to the minister so that he can check on it; I do not want to enter into any controversy with respect to it-that this man had retired from the naval service at his own request. I do not make this statement with any desire to defend the man who has made these charges, because I want to make it clear and have it distinctly understood that so far as we are concerned we are anxious only that should there be anything in these charges which will bring about a closer approach to perfection in our naval services, it should be looked into.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, February 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. W. E. Harris (Grey-Bruce) for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session and the amendment thereto of Mr. Graydon, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.
Mr. L.-Philippe PICARD (Bellechasse): Mr. Speaker, in rising to proceed with the remarks which I started to make last night I should like my first words to be words of welcome to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). I should like him to be assured that we all rejoice at seeing him back in his seat and in such apparent good health. We appreciate the considerable strain he is under at all times and the heavy burdens which he has to carry. Whatever may be the opinion of some of us about certain of the policies upon which he may advise the government, I do not think anyone will deny the extent of the service which he renders to his country at a moment like this.
There was an unforgivable omission in my remarks last evening. When I started to speak I wanted to keep my remarks as brief as possible because I knew I had only fifteen minutes before eleven o'clock. I omitted to congratulate the new parliamentary leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon). Many have wished him long life in his present position, but I cannot be that cruel. Let us say that we wish him a better fate than that of some of his immediate predecessors. Since he is quite young, let us say that we wish him to reach the head treasury bench when he is the same age as the only one of his immediate predecessors, who became Prime Minister, Mr. Bennett. Then after a short tenure of office, he could enter the House of Lords as Viscount Graydon of Peel.
In an effort to keep my remarks last evening as brief as possible I skipped from one subject to another and there were one or two remarks in connection with lease-lend which I postponed making. As I have a few minutes at my disposal, I shall make them now.
I have expressed my entire approval of the new set-up for lease-lend, and I do not intend to withdraw anything I have said in that connection. I should not like either that anything I will say now be construed as qualifying or conditioning what I said last night. It is said that we are to extend credit to any nation up to the amount they can pay and that we will then continue to provide goods as long as they are needed for the war effort or for the safety of the united nations. This
The Address-Mr. Picard

brings to my mind the fact that the control of one of the most important Canadian corporations is allegedly still held in private hands in England. I refer, of course, to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The railway problem in Canada has been one of our anxieties. Many remedies have been proposed by the railways and by the different railway groups, and there may be opposition to the plan I suggest.
I wonder whether it would be possible to do over there what has been done to a certain extent here. All United States securities at present held by Canadians are listed with the foreign exchange control board, and under the rules which now prevail the board can offer to Canadians a fair market value in Canadian funds for these securities. That would give the board, or the government, United States funds for the financing of our war purchases in that country. Why would it not be possible for the British government to do the same thing with shares of Canadian or foreign corporations-have them listed and get control of them, paying for them in English currency? That could be done without any disturbance to international exchange. These shares could then be transferred to the Canadian government, which would hold them as part payment for the goods we shall send to Great Britain under lease-lend. That would seem to be a perfectly normal and fair exchange.
When the United States gave to Great Britain fifty old destroyers, Britain in return granted the United States bases in certain British islands or territories which the United States considered necessary for its own defence. Those bases may be in the hands of our good neighbours for longer than a few weeks or a few years. Would it not be considered another fair exchange if financial control of one of our largest corporations passed finally int o the hands of Canada? Would it not simplify matters when the time comes that we shall have to face the railway problem in Canada if at that time the Canadian government, or an independent corporation under the government, such as the foreign exchange control board, owned or controlled the shares of the C.P.R. now held outside this country? It is a well-known fact that prior to this war and prior to the last war a considerable amount of this stock was held in Germany, France, Holland, and a large part of it in the British isles. Such stock as is now in alien hands is being taken care of by the custodian of enemy property. Would if not be possible to arrive at an arrangement with Great Britain for the transfer of such shares as are held in Britain, as an appropriate compensation for whatever we may do under lease-lend?
[Mr. Picard. 1
It also occurs to me that the Labrador question, which was settled so nicely by the privy council in 1926, if I remember correctly, might be the subject of negotiations, let us say, between the two governments. Not that I should like to pose as a Canadian imperialist or be suspected of a desire to promote Canadian imperialism. I see my good friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) smiling when I use the word "imperialism", because he knows how much I am against British imperialism as applied to Canada; I certainly should not like to advocate Canadian imperialism and spread that doctrine all over this continent. But would it not be a good opportunity for Canada to clear up the Labrador situation? There are vast water powers on the Hamilton river of which we were deprived by a scholarly judgment of the judicial committee of the privy council in 1926. Nobody would dare suggest that that body was tinged with political influences or affected by imperial policies; however, at that very time an imperial conference was sitting in London in which Newfoundland had a vote. But Newfoundland is now administered by the Secretary of State for the Colonies, and an arrangement could be arrived at granting Canada substantial benefits which, counted in dollars, would be considerable in years to come, if not at the moment. That might be a splendid gesture for the United Kingdom to make in return for what we may graciously decide to grant her under lease-lend.
When the house rose at eleven o'clock last night I was discussing the case of some young agriculturists who had been called up under the mobilization act. I told the story of one of these men, and I ended by saying that the board had decided that he should go into the army and that in the spring he could put in an application for six months' leave so that he could work on the farm in its busy season. But getting a release from the army is not as simple as it may appear at first sight, even when the man has a good case, and I will come to that in a moment. Lest some of my previous remarks be construed as disparaging the revision board sitting at Quebec I wish to state emphatically that I have the greatest respect for all members of the board, and especially for the chairman. I think that they deserve all possible praise for the manner in which they perform their arduous task, and they do it with a great sense of equity and justice. But their hands are tied by a lot of silly regulations, and on many other questions they lack immediate information on different government policies with respect to exemptions or deferments which may be given to farm hands and farmers' sons. I would

The Address-Mr. Picard
say further-this may sound personal, but I must express my feeling-that the board at Quebec is advised by a representative of the registrar's office who to my mind is the man least qualified to occupy such a position of trust. His very presence on the board is sufficient to take away any respect for the law and its administration on the part of anybody who may be appearing before the board.
In the case to which I referred a moment ago, this man, file in hand, was trying to impress on the board that the young applicant was hiding behind special privileges granted to industrial workers while all the time he was classified as B2, and when his class was called he reported and left the factory where he was engaged. He was given no special privileges as a specialist; yet this man who was advising the board was continually emphasizing that point. At every moment of the board's proceedings when I have been there this man has acted in the same way. I thought at one moment that his conduct might be attributable to the fact that his own name translated into English means "let us win"-but I afterwards discovered that he had not served in any war, so that that motive might not be applicable to him. My point is that if there are many men on the boards like this man it is not surprising that in some places there have been complaints against the boards from people engaged in agriculture. If agriculture is to be protected, clear instructions should be sent to all the boards and to all the officers, and such men as the one who represents the registrar before the board of revision in Quebec should be dismissed. As to the registrar himself in Quebec, I consider him an able and efficient public servant, who performs his duties conscientiously and well.
I spoke a few moments ago of releases from the army. That is a much more difficult problem. These boys who appeal for release have been sent into the army in many cases because of their ignorance as to the proper manner of filling out the information sheets sent into the registrar's office, or because they did not know that they could appeal from the registrar's decision, or because of a decision of the board based on incomplete information supplied by the applicant. In some cases the file is misinterpreted.
In some cases the boy may have been properly sent into the army and the father who is left on the farm may be injured or become seriously ill, or perhaps the boy's elder brother may be in that position, which makes the boy's presence on the farm necessary for its efficient operation. In either case
considerable correspondence and endless delays take place before you can get any satisfactory results, if any. I know that we should proceed carefully in this matter and that we should not permit anybody and everybody to withdraw from the army. There should be some way in which these cases could be rapidly eliminated, especially when the spring comes, the season when men are most needed on the farms.
I will not go into the detail that I had intended to about two cases which I know of. In one case there was a delay of six months; in the other, five months have gone and no answer has yet been received. There have been medical examinations by doctors; statements have been submitted as to the size of the farms, and in one case, although the father had become permanently injured, the son had not asked for exemption, but application was made later, and we are still awaiting the result. I refer to these matters to show the necessity of a clear-cut policy as regards the farm workers, and the importance of advising the boards immediately on this question, so that uniform decisions will be arrived at all over Canada.
All men in trades directly connected with agriculture should be dealt with in the same way. For instance, where a man is a blacksmith, and the only one in the neighbourhood, and you cannot find another one within ten miles, the consequences are serious if he is taken into the army; yet in one case it is admitted that he is necessary to agriculture, and he is given a deferment; in another case deferment is not granted. Or take the case of a man who is operating a flour mill, perhaps the only one for several miles around: one board may decide not to grant a deferment, while another board may say that he is necessary to agriculture and must be retained at his work so that farming may proceed in his district. Uniform decisions should1 be easily arrived at in matters such as this, if the government would send to each of the boards a straight and clear-cut announcement of policy in this respect.
There is another thing I would like to speak about while I am on this general question. It concerns those who for one reason or another are considered at fault under the mobilization regulations. A right move was the decision arrived at some time ago to give a chance to register to all those who had failed to do so. This privilege could have been better explained in the press, although it was something to have it. It should be extended, I think, to everyone whose position is not regular under the old
The Address-Mr. Picard

regulations. Of the men technically at fault, I would say that ninety per cent are in such a predicament because of their ignorance, or the ignorance of their parents, or lack of information which should have been supplied to them. They are now hesitant to regularize their situation, and procrastinate in doing so because they fear reprisals and punishment.
I think the department should declare an amnesty, let us say of two months, for all those whose situation is irregular. Give them two months in which to report in writing to the nearest district mobilization bureau. At the same time the registrars should send a further notice to all those whose cases are irregular, those who did not get their notices from their local post offices, those who have failed to report for medical examination, or those who have failed to report to camp. Let them know that if they come forward and report, their case and whatever requests they may make for deferment or exemption will be studied and decided on their merits, and let them have no fear of punishment and reprisals if they get to camp because they are in some cases many months late. Let them come forward: if they have a good case give them deferment; if not, let them go in the army, but without any special hardship or punishment when they get in. The results, I am sure, would be good throughout Canada, because this is not a problem peculiarly applicable to Quebec; from what we see of the results of registrations in many districts it is much more general. In this way we would clear up a false situation which exists now in many parts of the country.
To this new advice should be added the questionnaire which is sent to all men engaged in agriculture, and they should receive two copies so that they can retain one. At the moment there is this process. A man receiving a questionnaire fills it up; if he is deferred for six months or some other period, the present practice is to ask him to fill a new questionnaire if his category is called anew, or if the delay given to him has expired. If in the meantime there has been a change in the farm stock; if the number of cows or pigs does not exactly agree with the number given in the previous return, if the man has one acre more or less in hay or barley or potatoes than was indicated on the previous questionnaire, immediately it is assumed that the man is trying to cheat the government, and whatever he says afterwards is regarded with suspicion. If these matters could be clearly explained, if the proper information were supplied to everybody, there would be considerably less trouble. As a matter of fact I -received a letter yesterday from a registrar informing me:

In answer to your letter asking me to send you a hundred copies of the questionnaire for the use of farmers, I must tell you that I have adopted the policy of not sending out copies of this questionnaire except to the interested party himself, because in the past there have been a number of abuses which have caused us worry.
I thought that was a very inappropriate answer to send to a member of parliament who is asking for information on a public matter.
In conclusion I should like to impress upon the house the difficult situation in which some farmers find themselves at this juncture. They do not know how to plan their production for the next year. They do not know where they will stand so far as help is concerned. On the one hand they are advised by the Department of Agriculture to produce -more and more- which is good advice; on the other hand they face mobilization orders and varying interpretations in each district by the mobilization board. They do not know where they will be if they are without the help of their sons or their farm-hands. So far as production is concerned, they face a shortage in certain supplies which they need.
I had some trouble about the dairy question in my district, -where men have increased their herds and produced more. This is one of the questions mentioned by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) when he interested himself in the fate of the processors of butter, those who processed their butter at home instead of sending their milk to the dairies. He may have some trouble in his district because of lack of transport. We are nearer the city; we have not so much trouble in that respect, but above all things we need cans. We have no containers, and under the new regulations it is going to be very hard to get them because they are not so quickly made in these days. I have fortunately good news to-day, because in a letter I have received from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) he informs me that the production of cans in January was nearly fifteen times as great as it was in January of last year. Last year there was a real lack of containers throughout the country, and especially in our district, where people extended their herds, enlarged their agricultural and dairy production to meet the demand, and, having facilities for transport, thought it would be easy to meet requirements. According to the letter from the minister, last year, in January, one of the largest companies produced only 1,026 cans, while in January of this year, upon a specially urgent request from the Department of Agri-

The Address-Mr. Green
culture they produced 16,038 cans. If this goes on, and if the good offices of the Minister of Agriculture are exerted in the same proportion all the way through, we may be in a better position in the months to come. But at the moment our farmers in my district are suffering from this shortage. They used to spread their small production of home processed butter in the adjoining district in quantities of twenty-five or thirty pounds. Under the new rationing regulations they cannot do that; they have to dispose of their production wholesale. Some of these places have no cold storage, so that they are forced to produce less because they cannot find containers to send their product to the city, nor can they dispose of it under the new rationing regulations.
There is another matter to which I should like to refer while on the subject of rationing. It may not be exactly in my field, but it concerns workmen. It seems strange to me that men who are working hard in industry, who leave their homes in the morning and do not return until evening, are not given a larger ration of butter, let us say, than men who are idle, or, as is true of many, are doing nothing in their homes, or are office workers. The man who leaves home in the morning, or at night for the night shift, is usually unable to come home for his meals; he has to have sandwiches or other things of the kind, and he must have sufficient butter. If he has only a share of the family ration or of his own ration the meal will not be so appetizing. I wonder if something could not be done in that regard. It may be difficult to arrange it but I fancy it has been done in other countries. It might be possible to stamp the books of factory workers who are under a special strain, so as to give them some special consideration.
