I shall take only a minute longer, Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the house. Last year when we were discussing bill No. 80 I came across a passage in the British Hansard with reference to the question of agriculture, which I should like to submit to the house. In a speech, the Rt. Hon. Eugene Wason, chairman of the committee that considered relief to agriculture in Scotland, made this statement:
It should be represented to the military authorities-
That was in 1916, a year and a half after the war started.
-that any attempt to maintain or increase the food production of the country would be made
impossible by the further withdrawal of experienced workmen.
In conclusion, sir, may I say this. Let us not forget that the land is the first element that enters into the question of production. Farming is the primary industry and the most essential in carrying on a war, because the best trained men, with the best and most modem equipment, cannot fight on an empty stomach.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
While it is hard to realize, the fact is that this is the fourth war session of the nineteenth parliament of Canada, and since it is a war session I suggest that it is essential that, throughout its length, the members of this house should keep before them a clear view of the war situation. By so doing they will help the Canadian people also to keep a clear view of that situation. As I see it, the picture is this. The united nations are at last able to turn to the offensive. There have been victories, grand victories, particularly in Russia and in North Africa. We have some reason to take heart, but let us remember that behind us defeat is barely out of sight, and ahead are tremendous tasks. The year 1943 will be a year of fierce fighting, and fierce fighting means heavy casualties. Therefore, for this house and for the country, the most important part of the speech from the throne should be the last paragraph, which reads:
We have reason to be profoundly grateful for the improved position of the united nations. We must be careful, however, not to be misled by recent successes. The submarine menace has been growing, not diminishing. Decisive battles have still to be fought and won. For some time past, the movement of munitions and supplies overseas has been seriously restricted because of submarine activities. Until that grave menace is effectively controlled, there is always the danger that reinforcements and supplies in sufficient volume may not reach the battle zones. As areas of conflict close in, fighting will increase in intensity and ferocity.
I stress the next sentences:
The hardest battles, the heaviest sacrifices may be in the future. Only the utmost sustained effort on the part of all the united nations will ensure defeat of the axis powers.
With that warning in mind, let us look out across the seas. Canada is a nation facing both great oceans, the Atlantic and the Pacific. To-day Canadians look across the Atlantic and see a frightfully powerful Germany, which has yet to be beaten to her knees, a Germany dominating the whole of the continent of Europe. They look across the Pacific to Asia and see another powerful nation, Japan, dominating many lands, a nation which must be attacked, a nation which has already won great victories, a nation which is now coiled

The Address-Mr. Green
and ready to strike. Its premier showed this quite clearly when he said in the Japanese diet three weeks ago, as reported in the press:
Reviewing the first year of war in greater east Asia, Premier To jo asserted Japan "has completed the basis for certain victory". "Our position for both offence and defence has been completed," Tojo declared.
The former ambassador from the United States to Japan has written a book entitled "Report from Tokyo: a Message to the American People." That is a book which I suggest should be read by every member of the Canadian House of Commons. He points out clearly what we face in the Japanese military machine. He refers to it in these words:
I have indicated the surprise and the shock I experienced on returning to the United States to find how little the American people, as a whole, appreciate the dangers we face in fighting this machine, a machine which, without any shadow of doubt, firmly intends, after consolidating the areas it has temporarily occupied in greater east Asia, to attack countries in the western hemisphere.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the war situation which confronts members of this house and the Canadian people to-day, in the month of February 1943; and this picture of the war situation at once brings to mind certain subjects which should be considered by this House of Commons during the present session.
First, questions having to do with our fighting forces. We have been led to believe that our Canadian army in Great Britain will lead the attack when the continent of Europe is invaded. If so, and there seems to be no doubt of it, they are entitled to and should get training in actual fighting before they are called upon to lead that invasion. They will be attacking an army that has been fighting for nearly four years. One wonders why Canadian units have not been sent, say, to North Africa, for war experience. It is true that some officers and non-commissioned officers have been sent there. But why have no Canadian units been sent abroad as such? Why have the Canadian units been held so closely in Great Britain? One wonders whether it has been because that is the Canadian government's policy or whether it is because the Canadian staff overseas insist on keeping direct control at all times over all Canadian units. I would point out to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston.) and to this house that in any event such war training now would probably mean greater efficiency and far fewer casualties when the Canadians are called upon to lead in the invasion of the European continent.

One wonders, too, whether there are sufficient reinforcements in Great Britain to keep our Canadian army u,p to strength once fighting begins. We know there will be heavy losses. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) warned Canada of this in his New Year's message when he was reported as follows:
_ Prime Minister Mackenzie King, in a New Year's message, warned the Canadian people that "all our armed forces" will be in action during 1943 and that they "must be prepared for heavy losses".
There is concern across the country as to whether adequate reinforcements are available. This question is so important that I ask the government to give the Canadian people immediately definite assurance that adequate reinforcements are available, and to arrange for a secret session of the House of Commons at which the members may be given the facts with regard to reinforcements, such facts as cannot be given out to the public.
We also have an army on the Pacific coast. Their job is to fight the Japanese. Why have not units, or at least officers and noncommissioned officers from the Pacific army been sent to the southwest Pacific where they could learn by actual experience the best methods to use in fighting the Japanese? Such action would increase the efficiency of the Pacific army, raise the morale of the men serving in it, and promote good feeling between Canada and the United States and between Canada and Australia. In fact Major-General Odium, who is now our ambassador to China and was formerly our minister in Australia, went further. Late in November he advocated in Toronto that Canada send troops to the southwest Pacific theatre of war to assist General Douglas MacArthur. He is quoted as saying:
The best defence for this country is not a group of divisions sitting passively in Canada, but some additional force-even as little as one division-sent to General MacArthur, so that, on the Japanese tender southern flank, he may pass from the defensive to a vigorous local offensive.
General Odium was the first commander of the second Canadian division overseas. Whether or not he is right, the fact is that sooner or later Canadian troops will be fighting Japanese troops, and if forced to do so without some war experience, the result will be increased casualties and perhaps lost battles.
Then a further question in regard to the fighting forces: How can the officers commanding in the Pacific army be expected to keep their units efficient and to instil in their men the spirit of the offensive when they have in the units two kinds of troops, one group-

The Address-Mr. Green
who have enlisted for service anywhere, and half or more than half who cannot be sent out of Canada? Furthermore, those officers [DOT]commanding are put in the invidious position that their units must serve beside United States units the men of which can be sent anywhere in the world. Canada is put in an impossible position in that regard. I urge the government to change its policy, cut out all delay and all political considerations and change its policy, bringing in a realistic policy by making all Canadian troops, certainly all Canadian troops serving in the Pacific army, available for service anywhere in the Pacific area.
Another question is whether our navy is getting sufficient escort ships to beat the U-boat menace on the Atlantic, and if not, why not? Last week a startling statement was made in Toronto by Mr. Desmond A. Clarke, director general of shipping, in which he pointed out that men were to be taken out of other war industries in order to help build escort ships. He is quoted as saying:
And we need them right now (referring to the men) not for cargo ships but for fighting escort vessels. We must lick the submarine. There is no use building more cargo ships to have them sunk.
Why should the men of the merchant navy, men who are facing such great hazards, not be treated as members of the other fighting forces? Why should they not be given the same statutory right to pension, and why should they not get the same income tax exemption? I suggest that these are things that should be changed without further delay.
One final question concerning the fighting forces is whether the time has not come, in fact whether it is not long since past, for the awarding of all pensions on the insurance principle, which, as hon. members know, now applies only to men once they leave the shores of Canada. I suggest it is high time that all men serving in the active army were protected by the insurance principle with regard to pension. It is also time that steps were taken to protect from cancellation the insurance policies which our men had taken out before they enlisted or were called up. Great hardship is being suffered by many married men in that connection, and something should be done to remedy the situation.
A second subject that should be considered at the war session is Canada's position in the group of nations known as the united nations. There are many signs of the growth in Canada of a "small-power complex," a feeling that we must run along behind Great Britain and the United States. Take, for example, the government itself; it apparently is quite content to be left out of all the major conferences. Last year it had to be prodded into claiming a seat for Canada on the Pacific council. This question is vital for Canada, because we are at the parting of the ways. Canada can eventually become one of the most influential powers in the world. I do not say one of the largest; I use the word "influential," far more influential than perhaps our numbers would justify. But we never will if we develop a small-power complex; other nations certainly will not take us at higher than our own valuation. If there is not a change in that respect, Canada will have very little to say at the peace conference, and this might mean great tragedy for the Canadian people; many of them have definite ideas, and very sound ideas, as to what sort of peace they want. Yet the larger nations may decide on some other type of peace that prevents the kind of world Canadians want from taking shape. Canada, I say, must make herself heard, and heard in no uncertain manner, on these questions.
A third subject which should be considered is this: this house should insist that Canada's man-power policy be "work or fight." It is just as simple as that. The picture at present is that there is a shortage of men for agriculture, logging, mining and many other vital occupations, such, for example, as fuel delivery. At the same time ministers are actually talking about Canada reaching her full production. The Minister 6f Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) has thrown out the hint that it is questionable whether Canada can produce any more. I thought I detected in the speech of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) the other day something to the same effect. This is a great mistake, because there are still many Canadian people who are impatient and anxious to do their share in connection with the war effort. It is simply a matter of mobilizing them. Many cannot find a place; for example, older people, and men and women carrying on their ordinary work during the day who are nevertheless willing to do part-time work in the evening or during the week-end. Little or no attempt has been made to make use of their services. Canadians are begging for direction from the government, while at the same time some at least of the national selective service offices are carrying on in the utmost confusion and with the utmost delay; long lines of people seeking work cannot get any satisfaction, and apparently no one is able to give direction.
It can all be traced to the policy of the government of not quite a year ago, which was "the negative compulsion of restriction,"
The Address-Mr. Green

the same old policy that had been, used in raising men for the forces, except that it was described by a different name. It is really a policy of coaxing, threatening and bluffing, instead of courageously leading, and is exactly the policy we have had in connection with the raising of troops. As one looks back over the past year it becomes interesting to read again newspaper dispatches appearing on March 25, 1942, when this "negative compulsion of restriction" policy was announced, and to find this:
The government yesterday launched an extended national selective service plan designed to obtain from every Canadian the utmost contribution to the war effort through application of "the negative compulsion of restriction."
Then it goes on:
Fruit of months of planning under direction of the cabinet war committee, a series of orders in council was tabled by the Prime Minister, giving effect at once to the new regulations.
I am sure you will remember, Mr. Speaker, how excited and thrilled we were that Canada was really going to see action with regard to the use of her man-power. Then a couple of months later, in May, 1942, we saw another splurge, as follows:
Canada prepared to-day to take up the last slack in man-power, when it was announced by Elliott M. Little, director of national selective service, that all unemployable male persons, including persons on pension, must be registered within one week of June 1 and renew their registration every two weeks while not employed.
Important sidelight divulged by Mr. Little to a press conference this morning was that the government not only intends to dredge its manpower pool to the bottom, but may move war industry into sections where most unemployment is reported.	*
So we went along until August, when the Prime Minister announced new man-power controls. This was after parliament had gone home, and we read:
Prime Minister Mackenzie King on Wednesday night announced proposed new measures of control over man-power and woman-power designed to place "all but very old, the very young and the disabled" behind the war effort.
Then on August 31 we had more headlines:
Compulsory employment for all under new selective service; no transfers without permit.
Regulations under which every unemployed Canadian must seek work were announced to-day by Labour Minister Mitchell and Elliott M. Little, director of national selective service. They go into effect at midnight to-night.
The next thing we heard was that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) had gone to Great Britain. While over there he gave an interview, in the course of which we find these words:
. . . application in Canada of some features of Britain's man-power policy may be forthcoming

when he returns to the dominion. He described Britain's mobilization of men and women for service in the armed forces and industry as "a magnificent piece of organization."
Months before that, the British had gone much further than Canada, when they conscripted for national service, either in the armed forces or in industry, all men between eighteen and a half and forty-five years of age, with similar provisions for women between twenty and thirty. The Minister of Labour was to come back and make things hum. Well, he came back and then followed a quarrel with Mr. Elliott Little. So that we have drifted along under the same policy, which is typified by an order in council issued on January 28, 1943, amending the national selective service mobilization regulations. On December 11, 1942, an order in council had' been passed under which all men of certaip age groups who had not reported for service were directed to report by February 1. The order in council of January 28, 1943, just three days before the men were to report, reads in part:
And whereas it is deemed necessary for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada and for the efficient prosecution of the war that the time within which every designated man aforesaid is required so to report be extended. . . .
Then it goes on to extend the time until March 1, and I suppose there will be a further extension to April 1. I think the reaction of [DOT]the public to this man-power policy may be expressed in the words "disappointment" and "disillusionment". The government must stop dodging and twisting on man-power; it must give clear, courageous leadership based on a policy of "work or fight", and I am confident that the people will respond. Accordingly there should be no doubt about my support for the amendment to the speech from the throne, particularly the paragraph which regrets the failure-
.	.	. to provide an adequate plan for theeffective use of Canada's man- and woman-power.
Then I come to my fourth subject. The speech from the throne mentions the need for a scheme of social insurance which will constitute a charter of social security for the whole of Canada, and a committee is to be set up to study the question. This is all to the good, but there seems very little chance that any legislation will materialize at this session, which means that Canada will continue to hold her present unenviable position as the most backward socially of the Englishspeaking nations of the world. Many hon. members, in all parties, wish to see humane legislation placed upon the statute books

The Address-Mr. Green
without further delay; in fact they insist that this be done. I suggest that during this session, while this scheme of social insurance is being studied, at least two great needs should be met. Those are the needs of our old age pensioners and of the recipients of the war veterans' allowance. These people are in an impossible position at the present time, with the cost of living as it is, and I suggest that they should receive at least $1 a day if unmarried and $2 a day where the husband and wife are together. Moreover, the regulations should be amended with regard to their opportunity to earn some extra income. At the present time, as the War Veterans' Allowances Act is being administered, great unfairness is being done those old soldiers who are able to go out and get jobs perhaps for only a few months. The new age is here now; it is not coming after the war. We are now in the new age when humanity, rather than material things, should be our first concern, and a very good place to start doing something about it is by meeting these needs I have mentioned.
Then fifth and finally there is the attitude of the ministry toward this house, and in this I am sure I shall have some support from hon. members on the government side. Last year I had an uncomfortable feeling that the ministers cared very little what went on in the house, as long as they personally were not hurt too much; that the debates were allowed to drag; that the house was used as a sort of safety-valve while the cabinet did the legislating by order in council. The press gallery had that feeling, too, as well as the public; and respect for parliament fell. If this is not changed it may lead to the break-down of parliamentary government in this country. I could give many examples, but I shall limit myself to two. In the first place it has been said repeatedly by hon. members on all sides of the house that parliament should have at least some check on the orders in council and administrative orders that are going through the mill in such volume these days. Yet the ministry have not provided any means whereby such check can be exercised. It cannot be done satisfactorily in the house, but there is nothing to prevent the setting up of a committee of members to which these orders in council and administrative orders could be referred for consideration.
The Canadian people need the protection of parliament against some of these orders. For example, last fall there was the threat of an order being put through to force the early closing of small merchants' stores. In Vancouver, and I assume the situation was the
same in many other centres, this would have meant the putting out of business of many small merchants, most of whom are veterans, widows or men and women who cannot do any other type of work. The reason given for the proposed order was that these people could be used in the war effort. I have always had the suspicion that somewhere behind it all was some man accustomed to big business who may have wanted to get rid of the competition of these small merchants. Any private member of this house, I do not care what his politics may be, would have known at once that such an order was foolish, but it took the controllers a long time to find this out. In the meanwhile these small people were caused a great deal of unnecessary worry.
There are other regulations, such as those having to do with taxis, the rental regulations, the national war services regulations and the fuel orders. All these should be considered carefully by this house. In the last few weeks there has been a great deal of trouble in Vancouver with regard to fuel; this year, incidentally, we have been forced to stop boasting about our mild climate. The fuel controller issued an order last summer that sawdust could not go over a certain price. Many of the sawdust dealers decided that they could not carry on at that price, and they simply went out of the sawdust business. The controller was not worried about this; all he did was to pass the order and let somebody else do the worrying. Then there were no men to deliver fuel. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) was not worrying about that; it was up to the fuel dealers to get the men. The dominion government has got into the habit of stepping in, but not stepping in the whole way. They step in just far enough to make a great deal of trouble, and then let the people do the worrying. Fuel is a necessity. In the speech from the throne when the last session was prorogued on January 27, we find these words:
Where required, more equitable distribution of the necessaries of life has been ensured by the rationing of supplies to consumers.
This was not done with regard to fuel. In my city people suffered, and I think people died because they were unable to get fuel during the cold weather. This sort of business is not good enough for Canada in the year 1943. Yet we find the Vancouver Sun, a supporter of this government, reporting on a visit which Mr. Gordon, the head man, made to Vancouver on January 25, as follows:
Mr. Gordon did not hesitate to rap Vancouver authorities and the Vancouver public for failing to heed warnings which he said his office had sent out.
The Address-Mr. Green

He rapped them in the same tone in which he squelched speculative questions about future rationing of commodities and issued an implied warning to potato producers to bring out their potatoes.
Some of these moguls seem to have very little understanding of the problems of the small man who is the backbone of Canada, and their actions should be checked and checked carefully by this house.
My second example of how this government has flouted parliament is in connection with naturalization. The Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty) will be interested in this. In 1940 a committee of this house was appointed to review the defence of Canada regulations. I happened to be a member of that committee. During the hearings we found many questions having to do with naturalization and with the deportation of enemy aliens which needed careful consideration, and on August 1, 1940, the committee recommended:	.
Your committee, therefore, recommends that *t the next session of parliament a special committee of the house be appointed to consider and review the law relating to naturalization. Your committee is also of the opinion that the special committee should review as well the law relating to deportation and again consider and review the defence of Canada regulations.
At the next session, in 1941, a committee was set up again to consider the defence of Canada regulations, and was instructed to consider also the law relating to naturalization and deportation. It reported on June 4, 1941, as follows:
13. Naturalization-Deportation.
Your committee has received some evidence and has investigated these two important subjects in part only and, notwithstanding the fact that your committee has held a great many meetings, including on occasions two meetings a day, the limited time at our command has made it impossible to devote the time to these subjects which they require in order to enable a proper report to be made to the house.
Your committee therefore respectfully begs to recommend that at the next session of the house ;he law relating to naturalization and deportation and matters incidental thereto be the subject matter of a reference to a committee [DOT]of the house.
During the following session of 1942 I asked on different occasions whether a committee was to be set up to study naturalization and deportation, and it was my understanding that this would be done. However, nothing happened. This was bad enough, but when we came back here in 1943 we found, if you please, that on July 9, 1942, while the house was sitting, an order in council was passed amending the naturalization regulations. Important changes were made in the regulations having to do with the necessity of an applicant filing a declaration of intention. Later,

on September 23, another order in council was passed again amending the regulations. On January 14 of this year, just a little over a month ago, we find1 that an order in council was passed revising all the regulations under the Naturalization Act. All this has been done without any reference being made to the House of Commons. Apparently nothing has been done with regard to deportation, but perhaps we shall have an order in council on that subject popping out of the bag one of these days.
At this time both these matters are most important. The question of who is to be a Canadian citizen, what rights he is to have, how his fellow Canadians are to treat him and what we are to do with enemy aliens are matters that must be considered1 carefully. At the present time any enemy alien who is interned cannot be sent out of Canada after the war if he has been here for five years. That is the law as it stands at the present time. It is ridiculous and a change should be made, without further delay. I repeat that this is the time when the law should be carefully reviewed by parliament or by a committee of this parliament. Parliament and parliament alone should decide what is to be done in connection with these matters.
The subjects I have mentioned, the flouting. of parliament by the cabinet, the need for humane legislation, the "work or fight" policy -with regard to man-power, Canada's attitude toward the other united nations and the affairs of the fighting forces are vital subjects which should be considered by the House of Commons during this sessiou.
The year 1943 will be one of severe testing for the Canadian people. They have shown great strength, not only in materia' resources but in character, and they will see this year through with courage no matter what tragedies 'may occur. I have no doubt of that In return, however, they have the right to expect of their government bold leadership; they have the right to expect of their parliament, of this gathering of their elected representatives, the most careful consideration of all vital subjects, and may I suggest, consideration given in a patriotic spirit modelled on the spirit of our young Canadian airmen who wili be flying in the skies over other countries far from their own homeland during every day that this house is in session.

Mr. Speaker, in common with many hon. members who have preceded me I should like to express my great pleasure at the favourable turn of events in the various theatres of war. I am sure we are all heartened by the successes

The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
which have attended our forces and those of our allies in Africa and in the Pacific, and particularly in the Soviet Union.
I cannot help expressing regret that the speech from the throne made no mention of the gallantry displayed by the Canadian troops at the battle of Dieppe. The constituency which I represent is the headquarters for the South Saskatchewan regiment. The commanding officer of that unit has the distinction of being the first Canadian in this war to be awarded the Victoria Cross, and other officers and men of the regiment were decorated for bravery and devotion to duty.
I want to support the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) when he asks the government that an opportunity be given this house as it was in the British house to discuss the Dieppe operation. The administration itself can best judge whether or not such discussion should take place in closed or in open session. But opportunity there must be; for while the gallantry of the men involved left nothing to be desired, that cannot be said of the staff work of those who were responsible for conducting this combined reconnaissance. There are several things which we ought to be told as members of this house, either privately or publicly, and the first thing is why there was no preparatory aerial bombardment to soften up the objective. My information is that in the original plan that was the intention, but at the last moment it was deleted. If this be true, we should know why. We should know why men were landed at high tide and taken off at low tide at an hour when anyone who is familiar with the channel tides would know that these men would have to cross four hundred yards of open beach to reach their barges. We should know why tanks were landed on a beach facing a twelve-foot sea wall which had not been breached. In 1936 I spent a day in the town of Dieppe, and I would imagine that even aerial photographs would show the impossibility of scaling a sea wall unless it had first been partly demolished by aerial bombardment. What astounds me is not that none of the tanks got off the beach, but that those who planned the operation ever expected them to do so.
I think this house should have some information from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) regarding any reports he may have respecting the weapons which were used in this operation; and if there were found any defects in quality or quantity we should have the assurance of the minister that this matter is being taken care of.
A recent newspaper report indicated that General McNaughton told press reporters that the lessons of Dieppe had been invaluable to the British and United States forces in their recent landings in North Africa. But, Mr. Speaker, General McNaughton and the Minister of National Defence will have to go much further than that. They will have to give the Canadian people the assurance that the lessons of Dieppe will be of value to our own forces when they are called upon to invade Europe. To lose sixty-seven per cent of our effectives in nine hours of action is a grievous loss, but I believe that those who lost their loved ones at Dieppe will be encouraged if they can be assured that the sacrifices made there will result in the saving of thousands of Canadian lives when our troops finally invade nazi-occupied Europe.
I have said repeatedly in this house that the people of Canada will forgive the defence ministers and their general staffs many things. But there is one thing they will never forgive them. They will not forgive them the loss of a single Canadian life on account of either incompetency or lack of carefully prepared planning. We all know that some attempt will be made to invade the continent this year, and that in all probability Canadian troops will be the spearhead of that attack. Casualties are inevitable-heavy casualties-and I believe the Canadian people will bear those casualties with fortitude; but they will demand the assurance that every possible precaution in the way of aerial support and meticulously laid plans has been taken in order to keep the casualties down to a minimum.
I do not say these things, Mr. Speaker, in order to reflect upon any person or persons on the general staffs, but we may just as well recognize the fact that the man on the street no longer believes in the infallibility of military experts. Some of these military experts were the same men who told us that the Maginot line was impregnable, and that the Russian army would last only six weeks. With such catastrophes in our minds as the campaign in Norway and the loss of Singapore and Tobruk, the man on the street is fearful lest the traditional conservatism of the military mind should result in fruitless and unnecessary sacrifices of human life. The Minister of National Defence and the other defence ministers can do much to allay such fears by being very frank with this house, either in open or in closed session, and telling us something of the lessons that have been learned, of the precautions which are being taken, and of the plans which are being
606	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
laid to see to it that operations in the future will be successfully carried out with the minimum cost of human life.
The speech from the throne also makes mention of the Casablanca conference. I want to make only one reference to that. I believe there will be general disappointment that as yet the united nations have not stated in clear and unmistakable terms what their peace aims are. There are those, of course, who say, and they have said it in this debate, that our first job is to win the war, and that afterwards we can discuss the question of the world we want to build. But I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the winning of the war is to some extent dependent upon the kind of world we shall build afterwards. The people of the occupied countries and of the neutral countries, and above all our own people, wish to know what we are fighting for; and since the common people are paying for this war in blood, sweat and tears, they most certainly have the right to know.
In the past few months a number of things have happened which have done much to chill the enthusiasm of those who believed that we were fighting this war to establish the four freedoms in the world. There has been the recognition of General Mihailovic of Yugoslavia as against the guerilla peasants of his own country. There has been the recognition of the so-called Otto of Austria, who has been given permission to raise an Austrian battalion in the United States. There has been the sanctuary given to Prince Paul of Yugoslavia, a former nazi collaborationist now enjoying refuge in British Kenya. Above all, there has been the unsavoury deal with Messrs. Darlan, Flandin, Nogues and Peyrouton. Have we forgotten that these are the men who were responsible for the loss of British and Australian soldiers in Syria, for the death of British sailors at Oran and Dakar, and that some of these new-found friends of ours were responsible for the deaths of over one thousand United States troops at the recent landing at Casablanca? These pro-nazi collaborationists have had the Morocco radio turned over to them. The type of propaganda which has been coming from that source has been so vicious that even the state department of the United States has had to tell its own people not to take that propaganda too seriously.
The man on the street does not think in terms of subtle diplomatic distinctions, and he wants to know what we are fighting for. He wants to know whether we are seeking to destroy Hitler only to replace him with a lot of little Hitlers. Some will take the view that
{Mr. T. C. Douglas.]
these matters do not concern us here, that they are the sole concern of the United States state department and the British Foreign Office. I protest most emphatically against that view. This is a global war. Whatever affects the united nations in any one part of the world affects all. To-day Canadian boys are flying over almost every continent, and if blood is the price of having a voice in building the world to-morrow, then Canada has bought and paid for a place in the councils of the nations. I should like to tell the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the government that they will have the support of the great majority of the Canadian people if they urge upon the British and United States governments that there shall be an end of dealing with collaborationists, because we can convince the world of our good intentions after the war only if we take a firm and courageous stand during the war. The Prime Minister can render a great service to this country and the world by urging, particularly upon Great Britain and the United States, that the united nations shall state in clear and unmistakable terms what our peace aims are, and by showing the man on the street that we are not only seeking to destroy nazism and fascism in Germany and Italy, but seeking to destroy them wherever they raise their ugly heads anywhere in the world. The time has come when we have to get over having a colonial mind, when the government has to begin to conduct itself as befits the government of a self-governing nation within a great commonwealth of nations.
I should now like to come nearer home There are so many matters regarding which one might speak as affecting the welfare of our country in war time that it is impossible to deal with them all. I shall, therefore, confine myself to dealing with one subject, namely, the state and condition of agriculture as it affects the people of Canada and particularly the farmers of Saskatchewan. In doing this, may I say that the hon. member for Regina (Mr. McNiven) said the other night that those of us in this corner in private conversations do not talk the same way as we do on the floor when we are discussing government policy. Let me say that we do not say to every government member whom we meet in the corridors what we think of the government's policy. We do not think that is necessary; we take it for granted that the government members know what -we think of their policy. I would not think of wasting the hon. member's time or my own in trying to appeal

The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
to his_ reason to get him to leave the Liberal party. I have never really thought it was reason which kept him in the Liberal party.
The first comment I wish to make with regard to the government's agricultural policy is that it is apparent that there has been no satisfactory cooperation between the government ministers responsible and organized agriculture. On January 29 the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) stated the grain policy for the coming year. In the course of his remarks he said that the government had arrived at this programme after full discussion with the wheat board, discussion with the advisory committee of the wheat board and some conference with the provincial agricultural authorities and the Canadian federation of agriculture.

Then we shall be very glad if the minister will table the statement.
Now, as to the government's agricultural policy, it seems to have been bedeviled, ever since the war started, with a series of improvisations and a total lack of any long-term, careful planning. There are a great many .illustrations of this contradiction in policy, and it is rather significant that in all the speech from the throne there is no mention of the government's agricultural programme for the war period, but merely a statement of what they intend to do to help agriculture in the post-war period. This is significant for the simple reason that the government has not had a clearly defined agricultural policy for war time but, as I say, merely a series of improvisations and contradictions. Let us look at some of them.
Take, for instance, the contradiction of having the Minister of Agriculture and the food administrator saying to the farmers of Saskatchewan, we want you to increase pork production 70 per cent, and beef production and coarse grains by so much; and, on the other hand, the Department of National- War Services taking man-power away at such a rate that it will be virtually impossible to hit the target set by the Department of Agriculture. The man-power question is something that will have to be gone into in greater detail as the session proceeds.
On March 23 last order in council P.C. 2252 was tabled, which gave the right of postponement to any man who was essential to agriculture. It placed the responsibility, not on the man to prove that he was essential, but on the board to prove that he was not essential. I can speak only for the province from which I come, but in that province little or no attention was paid to that order in council. The board continued to call men, and I am not laying the blame entirely on the board. The secretary has said to me repeatedly, in reference to cases that I have referred to him, "We are given a quota each month by the military authorities." They are faced with divided responsibility. The Department of Agriculture said, leave the men alone; the military authorities said, you must get so many men a month. The board could not, therefore, pay attention both to the order in council and to the request of the military authorities, and undoubtedly for the last year in Saskatchewan the decisions of the divisional board have been dominated almost entirely by the officer representing the military authorities in that province. The result is that our

farms have been almost completely denuded of man-power. In some instances the last man on the farm has been called.
The Minister of Agriculture visited Saskatchewan in January and made a statement, as reported in the Regina Leader-Post, in which he said that the present regulations provide that any farmer can obtain postponement of military service merely by demanding it and showing that he is a farm worker. Well, nobody knows better than the minister how absurd that statement is. Suppose the farmer does demand postponement and suppose the board does not pay any attention to him; then what? In scores of instances men have made application to the board, and the board had so many of them that they did not even get to the man's application by the date on which he was supposed to report. He had, therefore, one of two choices. The Minister of Agriculture is saying something. He can make his speech afterwards. Let him sit up in his chair and dangle his feet until I make mine. As I was going to say, in many instances these men found that by the date upon which they were to report they had not heard from the board, and they had either to risk being arrested for failing to report or, if they reported, they then were out of the jurisdiction of the Department of National War Services. It was, therefore, absurd to say that any man could demand postponement. He could make application, and many such applications were made, but they were often not replied to, so that a man had no choice but to report. As the government knows quite well, when Mr. Milliken was appointed as agricultural representative, he was so inundated with applications that he simply threw up his hands and resigned in disgust.
The government has issued an 8-point statement in the matter. I hear them referring to the new regulations, but they are not new regulations. Let us get that clear. The regulations are the same as those contained in order in council P.C. 2252. What has been issued is simply an interpretative letter seeking to advise the respective boards how they shall interpret the regulations. Let me remind the house of two things. First, we have no guarantee that the divisional boards will pay any more attention to the interpretative letter than they did to the regulations; and, second, even if they do, in many instances the damage is already done. I think the government will have to go much further. They may have to take the drastic step of taking men out of the army and putting them back on the farm wherever the farm has been left without sufficient man-power to produce the

kind of things which the Minister of Agriculture wants to have produced in the programme which he outlined the other day.
There is no use in the minister or anyone else saying, as the Minister of Agriculture did last week, that we have a farmer representative on the board and that it is up to the board. The government cannot hide behind the skirts of the divisional boards. These boards either carry out the government's policy or do not. If they are not carrying out that policy, the government should dismiss them and appoint new boards; but if they are carrying out the government's policy, the government must accept responsibility for their actions. The sooner we get back to the place where someone in the government is responsible, and will accept the responsibility, of dealing with this situation, the sooner we shall have sufficient labour power on the farms to fill the quotas which the Minister of Agriculture has contracted to fill.
Take some other contradictions. The farmer has been bewildered and confused by differing advice and different suggestions which have been made to him. The Minister of Agriculture goes on the radio and tells him to hold his cattle, and not long after that Mr. Donald Gordon, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, tells him not to hold his cattle and chides him for doing so. One day Mr. Taggart, the food administrator, declares that it is nonsense to talk about butter rationing, and within ten days we have butter rationing. At one time the farmer is told to produce more flax, to get into flaxseed production, and now he is told we do not need increased flaxseed production. I have before me a copy of a broadcast, reported in the Western Producer of January 21, made by Mr. George Robertson, secretary of the Saskatchewan pool, in which he says that early last December, that is 1942, an agricultural production conference was held here in Ottawa, in which it was agreed that the acreage seeded to flax during the current year should be increased by more than one million acres, representing an increase of 68 per cent over last year's acreage. Repeatedly it was suggested to the farmers of the prairies that they should get into flaxseed production. In my own constituency I know of many farmers who paid from three dollars to five dollars a bushel for royal flax seed and now, according to the programme announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, apparently the government does not want the farmer to increase his flaxseed production. Many of these men will use the seed anyway, and we shall find next fall that we shall have quotas on flax-and there is nothing harder to store than flax.

The Address-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
We had a similar problem before in connection with coarse grains. Last year farmers were told to get out of wheat and into coarse grains, which they did. They put several million acres into coarse grains. To-day thousands upon thousands of granaries all over the prairies are filled with coarse grains which farmers cannot deliver. The farmer has a quota of twenty bushels to the acre, and he is lucky if he can get cars to ship them. He was told to produce coarse grains; he had every reason to think that if he did he would be able to dispose of them, but now he cannot dispose of them.
One more contradiction in this policy. We have frozen farm prices and, what is even worse, we have frozen the amounts of certain farm commodities that the farmer may deliver and sell, but we have done nothing at all to freeze the farmer'*, debts. The debt situation on the prairies, and particularly in Saskatchewan, has reached a point where something must be done. At the present time, farm debt in Saskatchewan-mortgages, agreements of sale, debts on implements and so forth-is in excess of $600,000,000, or something over $21 for every acre of crop land. I ask hon. members to realize the plight of a prairie farmer. He has in his backyard all the means to make some payment on these debts. But he cannot dispose of his wheat; he cannot dispose of his coarse grains; they are frozen. It is not his fault; yet the interest on his debt continues to accumulate even though it is not his fault that he cannot meet it. Last year the debt adjustment act of the province of Alberta was declared ultra vires, and consequently the debt adjustment acts of Saskatchewan and Manitoba were placed in jeopardy. A debt conference was called in Saskatoon last fall, and my understanding is that at that time assurance was given that some steps would be taken by the federal government to pass an order in council under the War Measures Act giving the provinces power to protect the farmers during this war-time crisis. But that order in council has not materialized. In the meantime the judicial committee of the privy council has concurred in the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada and declared the debt legislation ultra vires. The other day I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) what the government intended to do about the matter and was told that it is still under consideration. I suggest to the government that it will have to have more than consideration; some steps will have to be taken immediately to prevent all foreclosures
and evictions and to freeze debt. If the farmer is to have his prices and quotas frozen, then he ought to have his debts frozen. I say to the Minister of Agriculture in all seriousness that if the farmer does not get some measure of security on his farm, if something is not done about his debts, about his manpower-because he is to have less machinery- then we are headed for trouble. I know in my own constituency farmers are getting rid of their stock, in some instances men who have been trying hard to raise stock. I say to the minister that I am afraid that unless some steps are taken not only shall we not reach the objectives which we have set but we may not reach this year even the objectives which were attained last year.
That is why we in this group ask for a longterm plan mapping out the things to be produced and the quantities which the government is prepared to accept. We ask also for parity prices for the duration and for a period after the war. The average farmer cannot go into producing certain commodities unless he knows that he can count on a certain price over a period of time.

Of course he should, but certainly he should be guaranteed them now. If he starts certain lines of production at the suggestion of the minister, he should not find a year or two hence when he is ready to market the products that the price has gone. The slogan on the prairies has been: When there is a price there are no pigs and when there are pigs there is no price. We are seeking to avoid that.
The third thing we suggest is that the government should set up agricultural commodity marketing boards which would take delivery of these commodities from the farmer at the guaranteed price; dispose of them to the retail or export trade and absorb any loss incurred, as is being done by the wartime prices and trade board, which is subsidizing certain industries.
Fourth, we ask that sufficient labour be returned to the farms that are denuded, and sufficient left on the other farms, to enable them to meet the demands for foodstuffs that have been sent out by our allies.
Lastly, we ask that the government take steps to freeze farm debt and give the farmers security on their farms in this period during which they cannot deliver the commodities which they have produced.

In conclusion, one word with reference to the discussion of social security in the postwar world. We in this group have always maintained, and continue to maintain, that there cannot be such a thing as a system of social security superimposed upon a system of economic insecurity. There can be no social security apart from economic security. Sir William Beveridge makes it perfectly plain that when he is talking of a social insurance scheme it is based on more or less continuous employment. He says that any excess over eight and a half per cent of unemployment will throw his whole scheme out of gear. Therefore we believe that for anyone to talk, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) did yesterday about social security on the one hand and retaining free enterprise on the other is a contradiction in terms, because rugged individualism has never produced for our generation anything but ragged individuals on the one hand and people wallowing in wealth on the other. It is time we realized that to talk glibly about "social insurance" and "social security" and the "Beveridge plan" as though these things could be superimposed upon an economic system that has produced poverty on thd one hand and plenty on the other, natural resources needing to be developed on the one hand and unemployment on the other, is to talk about things that contradict each other. We believe that there can be no social security for the people of Canada until we are prepared to make fundamental economic changes and to reorganize our society in the interests of all the people instead of allowing it to be used as a means of economic exploitation for the benefit of a few.
In the magazine Time dated January 11, there is a statement by Monsignor John A. Ryan of Washington, an outstanding leader of the Roman Catholic church in the United States. He sums the position up in words which are very clear. He says:
The millions of returning soldiers and sailors will not be satisfied or fooled by the old claptrap concerning "rugged individualism" "American opportunity" or "American equality" . . . they will not be lulled to sleep by commonplaces about the limitation and difficulties of distribution, nor by promises of "prosperity just around the corner". They will demand jobs here and now. I do not believe that an economy dominated by the philosophy of "free enterprise" will be able to meet that demand.
